"Subject: Random brain stuff I wanted to fill you in on
Hey Sam,
Hope your o-chem midterm didn’t leave you curled up crying in the library bathroom like you predicted — that meme you sent of the guy sticking a pencil up his nose over reaction mechanisms had me cackling so loud my roommate banged on my wall at 11pm.
I wanted to circle back to that convo we had at the pepperoni pizza place last week, right? The one where we said we were sick of pretending all our random quiet moods are just ‘tiredness’ instead of weird old brain stuff? I had therapy yesterday and we spent the whole hour going over my triggers, so I figured I’d run them by you so you don’t end up confused when I zone out or bolt down a store aisle out of nowhere.
First off: cherry cough syrup. Smell, taste, even just the sight of that neon red bottle. When I was 12, my mom got that brutal pneumonia that landed her in the ER for three days, and right before that she was chugging that stuff every two hours nonstop. I was too little to get how serious it was back then, so my dumb lizard brain just tied that cherry smell to being terrified she’d disappear, y’know? Last week at Target when we were grabbing cold meds and I suddenly sprinted to the chip aisle? That’s why. Sorry I bailed on you mid-sentence without explaining.
Second: slamming doors, cabinets, even fridge doors, even if it’s 100% an accident. My dad used to slam every surface in the house when he and my mom were getting divorced, and for years I thought any loud slam meant a screaming fight was 2 minutes away. I know you’re a total chaos gremlin when you’re making morning coffee and you don’t mean to slam the mug cabinet, so I wanted you to know it’s not you — I just have to do that dumb 4-7-8 breathing thing my therapist taught me for 10 seconds before my brain catches up to reality.
And the last big one is people canceling plans last minute with zero context. My grandma used to promise she’d take me to the zoo every single weekend when I was 7, and she’d text my mom 15 minutes before we were supposed to leave saying she bailed, no excuse, every time. So now even if it’s a super casual ‘let’s get tacos after class’ plan, if someone hits me with a ‘can’t do it sorry’ with no follow-up? I get this stupid little rejected hollow feeling even if I logically know it’s not about me. For the record, that time you canceled our hike last month to drive your sister to the airport? Totally fine, no weird feelings at all — I’m talking the ‘eh I don’t feel like leaving the house’ texts with zero extra info.
I’m working on all of this, obviously. The breathing stuff helps a lot, and we’re doing low-stakes exposure therapy with the cough syrup thing (don’t worry, I’m not chugging it, just sniffing a travel bottle for 10 seconds a day lmao). I just didn’t wanna keep you in the dark, since you’re my favorite person to hang out with, and I hate that I’ve been weird about random stuff without telling you why. Also, for the record? You can dump all your triggers on me whenever you want, no judgment. I’ll memorize them, avoid them, bring you extra sour candy if you need it, the whole nine yards.
Come over tomorrow, I bought that blue raspberry sour candy you love and we can marathon that terrible pirate reality show we’ve been hyping up. Text me what time works for you.
Your favorite person who hates cherry cough syrup more than o-chem hates you,
Jesse"

# Muted Lagoon #729
(for anyone who’s ever been the in-between)

I’m the middle swatch on the dust-furred paint rack
at the Lowe’s off the highway,
where kids sneak in after school
to grab free swatches for collages
and hide from the rain when the bus is late.
The AC smells like sawdust and the cherry slushie
the greeter hides under the register.

The front bins brim with singles:
viral lavender, tangerine tingle,
the exact shade of that TikTok girl’s accent wall
everyone reposts to their room inspo boards.
These are the swatches that get torn free first:
taped to phone cases, slipped into locker doors,
used as bookmarks for dog-eared shonen manga.
I’m the one they skip.
Too green for the girl who wants sky blue,
too blue for the guy who wants forest green.
The in-between. The afterthought.
The one that doesn’t look cool enough for a feed.

Last week, a trio of juniors piled in,
hoodies slung over their bulging backpacks,
bickering about vegan cupcake flavors
for their anti-Valentine’s party,
joking that all three of them are singles
who’d rather binge Demon Slayer marathons
than text a dry talking stage.
They grabbed armfuls of neon pink and charcoal gray
to make party posters,
and I watched them leave,
their laughter fading down the tile aisle,
while I stayed stuck under the buzz of the fluorescent lights,
fading a little more by the minute.

*I would be the smudge on the back of your algebra notebook
when you scribble absentmindedly during third period.
I would be the border of your Phoebe Bridgers concert ticket collage,
the stripe you paint on your scuffed white Converse
when you’re bored at 2am and your mom’s asleep on the couch.
I would be the swatch you hold up to your face
when you’re picking out semi-permanent hair dye,
the color you name when someone asks what your favorite is,
even if no one else gets why it feels like yours.*

I thought I’d stay here forever,
crinkled at the corners,
until last Tuesday.
A kid with split black-and-blue bangs
and AirPods hanging loose around their neck
skipped the bin of popular singles entirely.
They ran their thumb over my matte edge,
paused for a whole ten seconds,
tore the whole strip free from the rack.
They tucked me into the pocket of their thrifted denim jacket,
mumbled to no one, “Exact color of the lake I sit at
when it’s too loud at home.”

I’m still the in-between shade
no one posts about on room inspo reels.
I’m still a little smudged around the edges
from months under the harsh store lights.
But for the first time,
I’m not just sitting on a rack,
waiting to be skipped.
I’m crumpled in a jacket pocket,
next to a crumpled receipt for sour gummy worms
and a half-chewed pen cap,
on my way to somewhere that feels like mine.

If you wander the UK’s most unremarkable city centre long enough—past the buskers who only play sea shanties about office admin, past the vending machines that sell single vintage buttons instead of chocolate, past the statue of the 1920s mayor who got caught stealing a goose from the town fair—you will stumble on a place called The Golden Palace. The city council keeps trying to zone it out of existence, claiming it’s a “glitch in the street grid” instead of a perfectly legitimate place to eat, but it never works. The Palace always stays.

**It is a restaurant, first and foremost—not a cloud kitchen that only delivers on full moons, not a pop-up toast stall that serves sourdough shaped like minor celebrity thumbs, not a food hall stand that charges £5 for a single bite of pickled turnip.** It’s the kind of restaurant where the booth vinyl is cracked in exactly the right shape to cradle your bad back after a full day of returning unwanted Christmas presents, where the background music is always a little too loud but never the wrong 90s Bollywood deep cut, where the waitstaff remember your order if you’ve come more than twice, even if your two visits were three years apart (once after a funeral, once after a punk show). There are no QR codes that make you sign a waiver before you can see the price of rice, no “experimental fusion” nights that pair tikka masala with matcha foam, no mandatory “community dining” tables where you have to make small talk with a guy who collects vintage parking tickets. It is a restaurant, the way your grandma’s kitchen is a restaurant, if your grandma’s kitchen had a flickering neon sign and a parrot that steals mint chutney off unattended plates.

**The food is Indian, stitched through with the weird, quiet magic of the city centre it calls home.** The butter chicken simmers for 12 hours a day, absorbing the hum of the nearby tram lines, the shouts of the street preachers yelling about the end of the world, the giggles of teenagers skipping school to get blue raspberry slushies from the corner shop. The samosa crimps are folded exactly the same way as the ironwork on the old town hall’s fire escape, and if you hold one up to the streetlight, you can see the same tiny, lopsided swirls. The garlic naan is so buttery it leaves a faint gold sheen on your fingertips, a tiny souvenir of the palace you can tuck in your pocket even after you leave. The chutney tray always comes with a mystery fourth pot that tastes like sunshine and forgotten 8th birthday parties; no one asks what’s in it, no one dares waste a drop. Rumor has it if you leave a half-eaten portion of biryani on the windowsill after closing, the city’s stray foxes will leave you a shiny trinket in return—last month a regular got a vintage pocket watch, the week before that a rubber duck with a tiny hand-painted crown.

**It lives in the city centre’s soft, unmarked spots, the parts the tourist board pretends don’t exist.** You won’t find it on Google Maps’ “Top 10 City Centre Eats” list, wedged between the overpriced tapas bar and the vegan doughnut shop that sells doughnuts shaped like famous philosophers. It’s tucked between a 24-hour laundromat that only washes neon socks and a newsagent that sells nothing but lottery tickets and vintage postcards of the city as it was in 1972. Hen dos, stag parties, and backpacker groups walk right past it, like their eyes slide off the half-burnt neon sign that reads *G LD N P L AC E* most nights. You can only find it when you need it: when you’ve missed the last train home, when you’ve just been fired over a Teams call, when you’re so hungry you’d eat a whole raw onion if someone handed you salt with it. No matter which direction you’re walking from, it’s always exactly three turns away, and when you leave, you’ll never be able to retrace your steps until the next time you desperately need a plate of aloo gobi and a mango lassi sweet enough to fix almost anything.

Regulars call the faint gold flecks the sign leaves in your eyelashes Palace Dust. They say if you sneeze it out while making a small, silly wish, you’ll get a free extra portion of poppadoms on your next visit. No one’s ever proven it wrong.

<<Biotechnology’s 2023 Echo: A Blog Post and Its Critical Reckoning>>

[Original Blog Post, published December 29, 2023, on TechVibe.co]
If 2023 will be remembered as the year generative AI broke into the mainstream, it’s also the year biotechnology’s long-building echo finally rippled out of sterile lab corridors into every corner of our lives. For years, biotech felt like a far-off future: CRISPR, mRNA, cellular agriculture, all promising big changes that never quite arrived for regular people. But 2023 changed that. This year’s breakthroughs aren’t just one-off wins—they’re echoes that will shape health, food, and climate for the next century.

Let’s start with the biggest echo of all: the FDA’s November 2023 approval of Casgevy, the first CRISPR-based cure for sickle cell disease. For 300,000 babies born with sickle cell every year, this isn’t just a drug—it’s a death sentence erased. What’s more, this approval opens the floodgates: CRISPR cures for cystic fibrosis, Huntington’s, even inherited blindness are just 2 years away, accessible to anyone who needs them. The 2012 paper that first described CRISPR’s gene-editing power finally landed as a real, usable tool for patients.

Then there’s mRNA, the technology that saved millions during COVID, echoing far beyond pandemic vaccines. In 2023, Moderna released trial data showing its mRNA flu vaccine is 40% more effective than traditional flu shots, with plans to roll it out by 2025. Even better? mRNA cancer vaccines are now in late-stage trials, with early data showing they cut melanoma recurrence by 44%. The echo of 2020’s vaccine miracle is rewriting the entire rulebook for medicine: soon, we’ll be able to custom-make vaccines for any disease, in months, not years.

Off the medical front, biotech’s echo shook up our food system too. In June 2023, the USDA gave final approval to Upside Foods and GOOD Meat’s lab-grown chicken, the first cultivated meat products cleared for sale in the U.S. This isn’t just a fancy restaurant gimmick: cellular agriculture cuts greenhouse gas emissions by 90% compared to factory farming, uses 99% less land, and eliminates animal cruelty entirely. By 2027, lab-grown chicken will be cheaper than conventional chicken, and by 2030, it will make up 10% of the global meat supply, ending factory farming as we know it.

Last but never least, 2023 was the year AI and biotech merged to create an innovation flywheel. DeepMind released AlphaFold 3 in May, a model that can predict the 3D structure of not just proteins, but RNA, small molecules, and even complex molecular interactions—cutting drug discovery time from 10 years to 18 months. Startups like Insilico Medicine already have an AI-discovered drug for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis in late-stage trials, and soon, AI will eliminate orphan diseases entirely by finding cures for rare conditions that big pharma once ignored.

The best part? Biotech’s 2023 echo isn’t just for scientists or billionaires. It’s for the mom with sickle cell, the farmer tired of factory farming’s pollution, the patient waiting for a cancer cure. This year, biotech stopped being a future fantasy and started being our present. The echo is only getting louder—and it’s going to change everything for the better.

---

[Critical Response to the Above Blog Post, published January 5, 2024]
The above blog post is a masterclass in tech industry hype: it takes real, meaningful 2023 biotech progress and twists it into a fairy tale that erases structural barriers, ignores peer-reviewed empirical data, and misleads readers about who actually benefits from biotech innovation. Let’s break down its most egregious flaws, one by one.

First, the blog’s treatment of Casgevy, the CRISPR sickle cell cure, is dangerously misleading. The post claims the cure is “accessible to anyone who needs them” and that cures for other genetic diseases are “2 years away”—but Casgevy is priced at $2.2 million per patient, a cost so high that even wealthy U.S. insurance companies are balking at coverage. What’s more, the treatment requires a myeloablative chemotherapy regimen that wipes out a patient’s bone marrow, making it unsuitable for 70% of sickle cell patients globally, who live in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) where 90% of global sickle cell cases occur. The blog also omits that 90% of the foundational CRISPR research that led to Casgevy was funded by U.S. taxpayer grants, not the private startups the post implicitly credits. The “echo” of CRISPR isn’t reaching the patients who need it most—it’s echoing only for wealthy patients and biotech shareholders.

Next, the mRNA hype is wildly overstated. The blog cites Moderna’s mRNA flu vaccine being 40% more effective—but that data only applies to 18-64 year olds, and only against flu strains that matched the vaccine’s design. Flu mutates rapidly, and mRNA vaccines have consistently underperformed against mismatched strains, just like traditional shots. The 44% reduction in melanoma recurrence for mRNA cancer vaccines? That’s from a small phase 2 trial of 157 patients, and 40% of phase 2 oncology drugs fail in larger, more diverse phase 3 trials. There is no evidence that mRNA will “rewrite the entire rulebook for medicine” anytime soon—most mRNA candidates for non-vaccine indications have failed in trials over the past decade, due to challenges with targeted delivery and immune reactogenicity.

The lab-grown meat claims are even more disconnected from reality. The blog states cultivated meat cuts emissions by 90%—but that number comes from industry-funded studies that assume 100% renewable energy for production and ignore the carbon footprint of specialized growth media. Independent peer-reviewed studies from 2023 found that current lab-grown meat production has a carbon footprint 4 to 25 times higher than conventional beef, due to the energy-intensive bioreactors and purified growth factors required. As of the end of 2023, Upside Foods’ lab-grown chicken was only available at two high-end restaurants in the U.S., selling for $20 a serving, 10 times the cost of conventional chicken. Scaling production to meet even 1% of global meat demand would require building $1.5 trillion in bioreactor infrastructure, a feat no independent analyst predicts will happen by 2030, let alone 2027. The “end of factory farming” is not around the corner.

Finally, the AI + biotech hype ignores the hard limits of computational tools. AlphaFold 3 is a remarkable research tool, but it does not “cut drug discovery time from 10 years to 18 months.” 90% of the time and cost of drug development comes from clinical trials, which test safety and efficacy in humans—steps AI cannot eliminate or even meaningfully accelerate with current technology. The AI-discovered drug from Insilico Medicine? It’s still in phase 3 trials, and 85% of phase 3 drugs fail to gain FDA approval. What’s more, AI models like AlphaFold are trained on existing biological data, which is extremely scarce for rare “orphan” diseases, meaning AI is actually worse at finding cures for rare conditions than traditional drug discovery methods for common diseases. The blog’s claim that AI will “eliminate orphan diseases entirely” is pure fantasy.

Worst of all, the blog frames biotech as a magic bullet that solves all problems without tradeoffs, ignoring the very real risks of unregulated biotech innovation: germline CRISPR editing that could create heritable genetic changes, biosecurity risks from synthetic biology that could create novel pathogens, and patent thickets that keep life-saving drugs priced out of reach for 90% of the global population. This kind of hype isn’t just harmless clickbait—it actively harms progress. It leads policymakers to divert billions in public funding to flashy biotech startups while underfunding the public health infrastructure and generic drug manufacturing capacity that would actually make life-saving treatments accessible to everyone, not just the wealthy.

P.S. If you’re tired of hype-driven biotech coverage that repackages corporate press releases as world-changing breakthroughs, check out independent outlets like STAT News, the Center for Genetics and Society, and the Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists’ biosecurity section for nuanced, evidence-based reporting on biotech progress and its risks. Biotech has enormous potential to reduce human suffering and combat climate change—but only if we prioritize equitable access and rigorous risk assessment, not just profit and hype.

This rubric is designed to evaluate laptops for everyday consumer use, including remote work, student coursework, casual media consumption, and light to moderate gaming, with a 100-point total scale split evenly between performance metrics and price-to-value metrics, so neither category overshadows the other for users who need balanced function and affordability. The performance category, which totals 50 possible points, starts with an assessment of day-to-day responsiveness, which makes up 20 of those 50 performance points, because even a laptop with top-tier specs feels frustrating if it lags during routine tasks. Testers will measure boot time from a full shut down, with under 10 seconds earning full marks for that sub-measure, between 10 and 20 seconds earning half marks, and over 20 seconds earning no marks for that specific metric. Next, they will evaluate multitasking responsiveness by opening a common set of apps, including Google Chrome with 10 open tabs, a 50-page Microsoft Word document, a Zoom call running in the background, and a streaming service playing 1080p video, with no frame drops, input lag, or app crashes earning full marks for this portion of the responsiveness score. Minor lag only when switching between more than 8 active apps earns 75 percent of the possible marks for this sub-measure, consistent lag during routine multitasking earns 25 percent, and frequent crashes or inability to run three or more common apps at once earns no marks for this section. The next 15 points of the performance category are dedicated to specialized workload capacity, to account for users who occasionally need to run more demanding tools beyond basic browsing and document editing. This includes testing video export times for a 10-minute 1080p video in Adobe Premiere Pro, with export times under 2 minutes earning full marks for that sub-measure, between 2 and 5 minutes earning 75 percent, between 5 and 10 minutes earning half marks, and over 10 minutes earning a quarter of the available marks. Testers also assess light to moderate gaming performance as part of this section, running two popular mainstream titles, Fortnite and Stardew Valley, at medium settings and 1080p resolution, with consistent frame rates above 60 FPS for both titles earning full marks for that sub-measure. Frame rates between 30 and 60 FPS with no major stutters earn half marks, while frame rates below 30 FPS or frequent crashes during gameplay earn no marks for that section. For users who do photo editing, testers also measure load times for a 50-megapixel raw image in Adobe Lightroom, with load times under 2 seconds adding a small bonus of up to 1 point within the specialized workload section, to reward specs that benefit creative users without penalizing laptops built exclusively for basic use. The remaining 15 points of the performance category go to battery life and thermal performance, which are often overlooked but critical for real-world use outside of a home office setup. Battery life is tested with a standardized continuous use test, where the laptop is set to 50% brightness, connected to Wi-Fi, and streaming 1080p video while running a background email sync and a single open Word document, with 10 hours or more of continuous use earning full marks for that sub-measure. Battery life between 7 and 9 hours earns 75 percent, between 4 and 6 hours earns half marks, and under 4 hours earns no marks for battery life. Thermal performance is tested during a 30-minute sustained workload, exporting the same 10-minute video used in the specialized workload testing, with the laptop’s external chassis staying under 35 degrees Celsius at the palm rests and keyboard, and no audible fan noise that can be heard from 3 feet away earning full marks for thermal and noise performance. Chassis temperatures between 35 and 40 degrees or faint fan noise under heavy load earn 75 percent, temperatures over 40 degrees at the palm rests or loud fan noise that interferes with phone calls or media playback earn half marks, and thermal throttling that reduces processing speed by 20 percent or more during sustained use earns no marks for that section.

Moving to the price-to-value category, which makes up the other 50 total points, the first 20 points are allocated to baseline value alignment, which compares the laptop’s tested performance against market rates for comparable hardware. To calculate this, testers compile the average price of laptops with identical or nearly identical core specs, including processor generation, RAM capacity, storage type and size, and display resolution, across major retailers like Amazon, Best Buy, and the brand’s official website at the time of testing. If the laptop’s retail price is 15 percent or more below the average price for comparable spec laptops, it earns full marks for baseline value alignment, if it is between 5 percent below and 5 percent above the average, it earns 75 percent of the possible marks, if it is between 5 and 15 percent above the average, it earns half marks, and if it is 20 percent or more above the average for comparable specs, it earns no marks for that section. Within this baseline value section, there is a small adjustment for build quality, where a laptop with a durable aluminum chassis, spill-resistant keyboard, or military-grade durability certification can earn up to 2 extra points if it is priced at or below the average for comparable specs, as these features add long-term value that is not always reflected in raw spec sheets. The next 15 points of the price category go to included features and long-term cost of ownership, which account for perks that reduce the need for additional purchases or extend the laptop’s usable lifespan. First, testers evaluate included connectivity and accessories: if the laptop comes with a full-size HDMI port, two or more USB-A ports, a SD card reader, and a compatible charger in the box, without requiring users to purchase separate adapters for common peripherals like monitors, external hard drives, or cameras, it earns full marks for included connectivity features. If it requires one adapter for a common peripheral it earns 75 percent, if it requires two or more adapters for routine use it earns half marks, and if it does not include a charger in the box at all it earns no marks for that sub-measure. Long-term cost of ownership also includes assessing the ease of repair and upgradeability, with laptops that allow users to replace the RAM, storage, and battery at home with standard tools, without voiding the warranty, earning full marks for that sub-measure. Laptops that only allow storage upgrades earn half marks, and laptops that have all components soldered to the motherboard, making repairs or upgrades impossible without professional, costly service, earn no marks for that section. Warranty length factors in here as well, with a 3-year or longer manufacturer warranty that covers hardware defects and accidental damage adding up to 2 extra points within this section, while a 1-year warranty that only covers manufacturing defects is considered the baseline, and a warranty shorter than 1 year results in a 2-point deduction, as shorter warranties increase the risk of unexpected repair costs shortly after purchase. The remaining 15 points of the price category go to use-case specific value, which adjusts the score to reflect how well the laptop meets the needs of its target audience, rather than applying a one-size-fits-all standard. For example, a budget laptop priced under $500 intended for high school students who only need to write papers, browse the web, and attend virtual classes is not penalized for lacking a high-end graphics card or 4K display, as those features would add unnecessary cost for its target user, and instead earns marks based on how well it delivers on the core needs of its intended audience at its price point. To assess this, testers first identify the brand’s stated target audience for the laptop, whether that is budget students, remote professionals, content creators, or gaming enthusiasts, then compare its features and performance against the top priorities of that group, with a laptop that meets 90 percent or more of the core needs of its target audience at a price point 10 percent or below the average for that use case earning full marks for use-case specific value. If a laptop meets 70 to 89 percent of its target audience’s core needs and is priced within 10 percent of the average for that use case, it earns 75 percent of the possible marks, if it meets 50 to 69 percent of core needs or is priced 10 to 20 percent above the average for its use case, it earns half marks, and if it meets fewer than 50 percent of its target audience’s core needs or is priced 20 percent or more above the average for that use case, it earns no marks for that section. There is also a small penalty for misleading marketing claims within this section, for example, if a brand advertises a laptop as a “gaming device” but it cannot run even casual games at 30 FPS, or advertises “all-day battery life” but only delivers 3 hours of continuous use, that results in a 3-point deduction from the use-case value score, as deceptive marketing erodes the overall value of the product for consumers who purchase it based on those claims.

Once all performance and price points are tallied, the total score translates to a clear performance and value rating that consumers can use to make purchasing decisions. A total score of 90 to 100 indicates an exceptional laptop that offers class-leading performance at an outstanding price point, with no major flaws that would detract from everyday use, and is a top recommendation for almost any user in its target audience. A score of 80 to 89 indicates a very good laptop that offers strong performance and solid value, with only minor drawbacks like slightly loud fan noise under load or a single missing port that most users can work around easily. A score of 70 to 79 indicates a good laptop that meets most basic needs at a fair price, but may have noticeable tradeoffs like shorter battery life or limited upgradeability that users should consider before purchasing, especially if they plan to use the laptop for more than 2 or 3 years. A score of 60 to 69 indicates a below-average laptop that either has lackluster performance for its price or is overpriced for the specs it offers, and is only recommended if it is on sale for at least 20 percent below its retail price to offset its shortcomings. A score below 60 indicates a poor value laptop that either has severe performance issues that make routine use frustrating, is drastically overpriced for its features, or both, and should be avoided by most consumers in favor of better options at the same price point. To ensure the rubric remains fair as technology evolves, all baseline spec averages and performance thresholds are updated every six months to account for new processor releases, drops in component prices, and shifts in standard consumer expectations, so a laptop that scored well two years ago is held to the same standard as new releases when re-evaluated for current purchase recommendations. Additionally, testers will adjust use-case priority rankings as consumer needs shift, for example, as more users rely on cloud storage for their files, local storage capacity may become a less heavily weighted factor for budget student laptops, while battery life and webcam quality for virtual classes may become more important, to ensure the rubric continues to reflect the actual needs of people shopping for laptops in the current market.

I’d been pushing for a new personal best, my breath coming in steady puffs and my workout playlist thumping in my earbuds, when a sharp, echoing CRUNCH from the thick underbrush 15 feet to my left ripped me right out of my rhythm.

I ripped out my earbuds, my heart hammering so hard I could feel it in my fingertips, and squinted into the long, stretching shadows—until two glowing, amber eyes blinked back at me. For a split, panicky second, I thought it was a coyote, or even a lost black bear, like the ones the local parks department had been issuing alerts about all month. But then a massive 12-point buck stepped into the slanted orange glow of the setting sun, its antlers so wide they almost brushed the oak branches on either side of it.

I’d seen dozens of deer on this trail over the years, but never one this big, never one that didn’t bolt the second it caught a whiff of human sweat or cherry energy gel. I’d read a hiking blog the week prior that rutting season made male deer unpredictable, even aggressive, so I locked my knees and held perfectly still, not even daring to swallow too loud for fear of spooking him. ### Section 1
Elias Voss had worked the front desk of the Hawthorne District Public Library’s rare book room for three years before he met Maren Hale, and in that time, he’d developed a rigid, unchanging routine that he’d once bragged to his sister could survive a Category 5 hurricane or a surprise visit from their overly critical grandmother. He brewed chamomile tea at exactly 9:02 a.m. every weekday, timed so the steam stopped curling right as the first regulars wandered in. He arranged the brass library bookmarks by weight every morning, from the tiny, delicate leaf-shaped ones to the heavy vintage ones engraved with the library’s 1905 founding date. He wiped down the oak reading table with lemon oil every afternoon at 3:15, following the grain so carefully he could trace every scratch and water ring from memory. He even counted the 17 steps from the break room to the front desk every shift, noting the crack in the linoleum at step 12 that the city had been promising to fix for six months. His routine was his comfort, a set of small, predictable joys that kept the chaos of the world at bay, until Maren walked through the door on a rainy Tuesday in April. She was wearing faded canvas overalls stiff with milkweed sap, mud caked on the toes of her work boots, and a silver hoop earring shaped like a bumblebee dangling from her left ear. A tattoo of a monarch butterfly curled up her right forearm, peeking out from the sleeve of her flannel shirt, and she was clutching a crumpled list of book titles in one hand. She apologized profusely for tracking mud into the rare book room, gesturing at her boots with a sheepish grin, and Elias waved her off, telling her the library had seen far worse messes, including the time a retiree spilled a full bottle of maple syrup on a first edition of *Where the Wild Things Are* during a storytime event. She laughed, a bright, loud sound that echoed off the high, book-lined walls, and asked if he had a copy of the 1912 edition of *Pacific Northwest Wildflower and Pollinator Field Manual*, explaining that she ran a volunteer project restoring native pollinator corridors in the vacant lots along Burnside Street. Mid-sentence, she blinked hard, jerked her left shoulder up to her ear, and barked “HONEYCOMB!” so loud it made the brass bookmarks rattle on the desk. Elias didn’t flinch. He didn’t stare, or apologize, or ask if she was okay, or do any of the things most people did when they saw a tic for the first time. He just nodded, said “One sec, I know right where that is,” and turned to pull the leather-bound volume from the locked shelf behind him. Elias’s 12-year-old cousin Leo had been diagnosed with Tourette Syndrome when he was seven, so Elias had spent years learning not to react to tics, to treat them like any other harmless quirk, like Leo’s habit of chewing on the end of his hoodie string or his obsession with Minecraft. When Elias turned back with the book, Maren was staring at him, wide-eyed, like she’d just seen a ghost. “You didn’t… say anything,” she said, tilting her head, like she was trying to figure out if he was being polite or if he just hadn’t noticed. “About the tic, I mean.” Elias shrugged, setting the book on the table and pushing it toward her. “My cousin has Tourette’s. I’m used to random outbursts. Last week he yelled ‘CREEPER!’ mid-dinner and spilled his whole glass of lemonade on my mom’s new tablecloth.” Maren laughed again, this time softer, a little relieved, and explained that her tics were almost always related to plants or bugs, a quirk her neurologist said came from spending 90% of her waking hours thinking about pollinators. She had motor tics too, she said: shoulder jerks, three quick finger snaps, a sharp nod of the head, but the vocal tics were the ones that made people stare the most. She stayed for two hours that day, flipping through the field manual and taking notes in a beat-up leather notebook covered in bee stickers, and when she left, she pressed a monarch butterfly sticker into the palm of his hand as a thank you. Elias stuck that sticker on the corner of his name tag the second she was gone, and it stayed there, faded and peeling at the edges, for the next two years. Maren came back every Tuesday after that, always at 10 a.m., always wearing overalls, always bringing him a small gift: a jar of wild blackberry jam she’d made, a pressed milkweed bloom, a sticker of a bumblebee holding a tiny book. Elias started saving her rare botanical books as soon as they came in, tucking them behind the desk so no one else could check them out, and he started looking forward to Tuesdays more than any other day of the week, more than his monthly bookbinding workshop, more than the weekend video game marathons with Leo, more than the chamomile tea he brewed every morning. He’d never admit it to his sister, but his carefully curated routine had started to revolve around Maren, and he didn’t mind one bit.

### Section 2
The first time Maren invited Elias to join her for a volunteer planting day, he’d spent 45 minutes the night before picking out work clothes that didn’t look like he’d tried too hard, settling on faded gray work pants and a frayed navy flannel he’d owned since his sophomore year of college. He’d even bought a new pair of work boots, because his old sneakers were full of holes and he didn’t want to step on a thorn or a piece of broken glass in the vacant lot. The planting day was cold and drizzly, the kind of soft Portland rain that seeps through your jacket before you even notice it’s falling, and when Elias arrived, Maren was already there, surrounded by a dozen teens from the local high school’s environmental club, passing out trowels and packets of milkweed seeds. She was wearing a neon yellow rain jacket with “Save the Bees” printed on the back, her hair pulled back in a messy braid dotted with dandelion petals, and she waved so hard when she saw him that she dropped the stack of seed packets she was holding. The teens didn’t even glance up when she jerked her shoulder and yelled “DANDELION!” as she knelt to pick up the seeds, just kept chatting and laughing as they dug holes in the soft, damp dirt. Elias learned that day that all the teens in Maren’s program were kids who’d been labeled “difficult” by their schools: some had ADHD, some were autistic, some had anxiety, all of them had been told they were too loud or too distracted or too “much” for traditional classroom settings. Maren told him later that she’d started the program specifically for those kids, because she’d been labeled “difficult” too, back when her elementary school teachers thought her tics were her acting out for attention, when kids would tease her and call her “crazy” for yelling random words in class. She said the plants never judged her, never asked her to be quieter or calmer or different, so she’d decided to build a space where kids could feel the same way. By the end of the planting day, Elias’s knees were muddy, his hands were blistered, and he’d helped plant 72 milkweed shoots and 40 native wildflower plugs, and he’d had more fun than he’d had in years. After the teens left, Maren suggested they get tacos at the food truck down the street, the one with the vegan al pastor that she swore was the best in the city. They sat at a rickety plastic picnic table under a faded awning, eating tacos and talking about the library’s upcoming rare book exhibit, when a man in a business suit sitting at the next table glanced over at Maren when she jerked her head and yelled “SUNFLOWER!” mid-sentence. He snickered, nudged the friend sitting next to him, and said loud enough for both of them to hear, “Can’t she control that? Jesus, people will bring anything out in public these days.” Maren’s face fell, and she stared down at her taco, suddenly quiet, like she was used to comments like that, like they still stung even after all these years. Elias didn’t yell at the man, didn’t make a big scene, didn’t even look at him. He just moved his chair a few inches to the right, so he was sitting between Maren and the man, and asked her to tell him more about the tiny blue mason bees she’d been talking about earlier, the ones that nested in the hollow stems of raspberry bushes. Maren looked up at him, her eyes a little shiny, and started talking again, slowly at first, then faster, getting excited as she explained how mason bees were better pollinators than honeybees for native plants. When they finished their tacos, Elias ordered her an extra side of guacamole, her favorite, and they walked back to his apartment, their boots squelching in the rain puddles on the sidewalk. Elias’s cat Mabel, a chonky orange tabby with a white paw that looked like a sock, was waiting for them by the door, and she rubbed against Maren’s leg the second she walked in, purring so loud it sounded like a tiny engine. Maren knelt down to pet her, and when she snapped her fingers three times, a motor tic she got when she was happy, Mabel just nudged her hand for more pets, completely unfazed. They spent the rest of the night sitting on Elias’s couch, listening to old Joni Mitchell records and flipping through Maren’s field notebook, which was full of detailed drawings of bees and wildflowers, scribbled notes about bloom times and nesting habits, and little doodles of bumblebees wearing tiny hats. They kissed for the first time that night, halfway through a song about clouds, and mid-kiss, Maren jerked her shoulder and chirped “CLOVER!” so close to his ear that it made him laugh. He pulled back, grinning, and said “That’s a good one. I like clover.” Maren laughed too, a little shaky, like she’d been worried he’d pull away or be weirded out, and she kissed him again, harder this time. They started dating regularly after that, fitting each other into their routines like they’d been doing it their whole lives. Maren would come to the library during his shifts, sit at the reading table and press flowers for the library’s new botanical display, and leave sticky notes with bee jokes on his desk when she left. Elias would go to her planting days every Saturday, bring donuts for the teens, and carry extra water bottles and band-aids in his backpack for anyone who needed them. On Sunday mornings, they’d make pancakes in Elias’s tiny kitchen, and Maren would have a tic where she flipped the spatula three times before flipping each pancake, so Elias started counting along under his breath, one, two, three, flip, like it was a little game they played. Elias’s sister teased him that he was smitten, that he’d turned into one of those guys who talks about his girlfriend every five minutes, and he didn’t even deny it.

### Section 3
Maren got the email inviting her to be the keynote speaker at the Pacific Northwest Native Pollinator Summit on a Tuesday, right as she was leaning against the front desk of the rare book room, telling Elias about the baby bumblebee queen she’d spotted in the lot off 28th Avenue that morning. She’d been checking her email on her phone while she talked, and she froze mid-sentence, her eyes going wide, before she slammed her phone shut and shoved it in her overalls pocket. “Nope,” she said, shaking her head, her voice tight. “No way. I’m not doing it.” Elias frowned, leaning forward across the desk. “Not doing what? Did something happen?” Maren sighed, pulling her phone back out and sliding it across the desk to him, so he could read the email. The summit was the biggest environmental conference in the region, with more than 300 attendees, including grant officers from the state’s largest environmental foundation, who were giving out $500,000 grants for community conservation projects. The keynote spot was a huge honor, and it would give Maren 45 minutes to pitch her pollinator corridor project to exactly the people who could fund it for the next five years, letting her expand to 20 more vacant lots, hire three part-time staff, and launch a free summer camp for the kids in her program. But Maren was terrified. She told Elias about the last time she’d given a public talk, back when she was in college, speaking to a small class of 20 environmental science students. She’d been so nervous that her tics had been worse than ever: she’d yelled “TREE BARK!” 17 times, jerked her shoulder so hard she knocked over a pitcher of water, and one of her professors had stopped her mid-talk to ask if she needed to go to the hospital. The whole class had stared, and she’d run out of the lecture hall and didn’t come back to campus for a week, too embarrassed to show her face. She said people never took her seriously when she ticced during talks, that they thought she was unprofessional or unstable, that they’d never give a half-million dollar grant to someone who yelled random plant names in front of a crowd. Elias didn’t tell her it would be fine, didn’t tell her to just calm down, didn’t tell her to try to control her tics, because he knew all those things were useless, that they just made people with Tourette’s feel worse. Instead, he asked her what she needed, what would make this feel less scary. Maren thought for a minute, then shrugged, saying she didn’t know, that she wanted to do the talk, wanted the grant more than anything, but she was so scared of humiliating herself that she wanted to say no. Elias came up with a plan that night, after they’d eaten takeout pasta and watched a documentary about bees. They’d practice the talk every night for a month, in the rare book room after closing, when the library was empty and quiet. He’d set up a fake podium out of a stack of old encyclopedias, sit in the back row, and act like a tough, unforgiving audience. When she ticced mid-sentence, he wouldn’t react, just nod and gesture for her to keep going. They also added a line to the very start of her talk: “I have Tourette Syndrome, so you might hear me yell random plant or bug names, or see me jerk my shoulder or snap my fingers. None of it is a reaction to anything you’re doing, and I’ll get right back to the point, I promise.” Maren said that line made her feel better, like she was taking control of the narrative instead of letting people make their own assumptions about her. They practiced every night, just like Elias said, and after the first week, they started bringing in guest audiences to make it more realistic: first Elias’s sister, then Leo, then the teens from Maren’s program. Leo came to one practice, and when Maren yelled “TREE BARK!” mid-sentence, Leo yelled back “ROCK!” one of his own most common vocal tics, and they spent ten minutes just yelling random words at each other, laughing so hard they cried, until Elias reminded them they were supposed to be practicing. The week before the conference, Maren’s tics got worse, spiking from a tic every few minutes to a tic every 30 seconds, her vocal tics louder than ever, her shoulder jerks so hard they made her arm ache. She got so frustrated one night, halfway through a practice run, that she threw her cue cards across the room and sat down on the floor, crying, saying she was going to cancel, that she couldn’t do this, that she was just going to make a fool of herself. Elias sat down next to her on the floor, pulled her into his arms, and let her cry until she calmed down. He told her that her tics weren’t a flaw, that they were just part of her, the part that loved plants and bugs so much her brain couldn’t even keep the names inside when she was excited. He said the people who mattered would listen to what she was saying, not how she was saying it, and the people who didn’t listen weren’t the people who got to decide if her work was good. Maren wore a dress made of organic cotton, dotted with wildflower prints, and Elias wore a suit with a bumblebee boutonniere. Leo was the best man, and during his toast, he yelled “MINECRAFT!” mid-sentence, and everyone laughed, because by then all their friends and family were used to tics, used to random outbursts, used to rolling with it. # Pitch Deck: MeepleMeet
Tagline: Your Home for Every Board Game Moment
12-Slide Pre-Seed Pitch Deck | For Angel Investors & Hobby Tech VCs

---

## Slide 1: Title Slide
### Key Content:
- MeepleMeet Logo (stylized meeple icon with a speech bubble)
- Tagline: Your Home for Every Board Game Moment
- Presented by: Jane Doe, CEO & Co-Founder
- Contact: jane@meeplemeet.app | @meeplemeet
### Speaker Notes:
"Hi everyone, I’m Jane Doe, CEO of MeepleMeet. Today we’re here to talk about the $31B global board game hobby, and the gaping hole in dedicated, end-to-end social infrastructure for the 150M+ board game players around the world."

---

## Slide 2: The Problem
### Key Content:
The global board game community is fragmented, underserved, and locked into clunky, general-purpose tools:
1. **Fragmented Discovery & Connection**: Players bounce between BoardGameGeek (database-only, 20-year-old UI), Facebook Groups, Discord, and Reddit with no unified space for social connection, local meetups, and hobby tracking.
2. **Painful Playgroup Matching**: New, 68% of casual board game players report struggling to find local playgroups that match their skill level, schedule, and play style (source: 2024 BoardGameGeek Community Survey)
3. **No End-to-End Game Night Tooling**: Players use 5+ separate tools (Google Calendar, SignUpGenius, GroupMe, physical score pads, rule books for game nights, with zero integration.
4. **No Accessibility-First Matching**: Neurodivergent, disabled, and new players have no dedicated way to find playgroups that accommodate sensory needs, wheelchair access, or rule explanation support.
5. **Underserved Stakeholders**: Local game stores (FLGS), publishers, and board game creators lack a dedicated space to connect directly with their target audience, sell event tickets, and promote releases.
### Speaker Notes:
"Right now, if you want to play a physical board game with people you actually enjoy playing with, you have to jump through 7 different hoops. And if you’re a local game store or creator, there’s no way to reach your exact audience without fighting general social media algorithms that prioritize viral content over niche hobby needs.

---

## Slide 3: Our Solution
### Key Content:
MeepleMeet is the first mobile-first, end-to-end social network built exclusively for the global board game community, serving every part of the hobby journey:
- Hyper-personalized playgroup matching for in-person and remote play, with accessibility and play style compatibility scoring
- Integrated game night hub with digital scorekeeping, rule reference, RSVP tracking, and post-game recaps
- Dedicated profiles and monetization tools for FLGS, publishers, and board game content creators
- Built-in collection tracking, personalized game recommendations, and niche hobby groups
### Speaker Notes:
"We built MeepleMeet to be the one-stop shop for every board game moment. Whether you’re a new player looking for your first casual Catan night, a competitive tournament player looking for a tournament, a local game store promoting your next open play, or a creator sharing your latest miniature paint job, MeepleMeet is built for you.

---

## Slide 4: Market Size
### Key Content:
#### TAM: $45B Global Board Game Ecosystem (projected 2028, Grand View Research)
Covers players, publishers, FLGS, content creators, and event organizers
#### SAM: 150M Global Monthly Active Board Game Players
40M+ dedicated hobbyists, 110M casual players who play 1+ times per month
#### SOM: 2M Active Users | $36M Annual Revenue by Year 3
### Speaker Notes:
"This isn’t a tiny niche hobby. Board games grew 20% during the pandemic, and growth has stayed steady as players crave in-person, low-screen social connection. We’re targeting a massive, fast-growing market that has never had a dedicated social network built for it.

---

## Slide 5: Product Overview
### Key Content:
Core Features by User Segment:
1. **For Players**:
   - Custom profiles with collection tracking, play history, play style preferences, and accessibility needs
   - AI-powered compatibility scoring (92% match accuracy in beta)
   - Game Night Hub with RSVPs, bring lists, digital scorekeeping, and shareable recaps
2. **For FLGS & Publishers**:
   - Dedicated business profiles with event ticketing, tournament signups, pre-order tools, and local audience analytics
3. **For Creators**:
   - Creator profiles with monetization tools, no algorithm penalties for niche board game content, and affiliate integration
### Speaker Notes:
"Our AI compatibility algorithm doesn’t just match you based on what games you like—it matches you based on how you like to play. If you hate rule lawyers, love casual play, or need sensory-friendly game nights, our algorithm finds you the perfect group. And for stores and creators, we give them tools no other platform offers to reach their exact audience.

---

## Slide 6: Pre-Launch Traction
### Key Content:
(Pre-launch, no public launch pending funding)
- 12,400+ pre-launch waitlist signups across 17 countries
- 42 FLGS partnerships across the US and Canada signed on for launch
- 8 indie board game publishers (including Stonemaier Games partner for exclusive playtest access
- 120+ board game content creators (10k+ followers each) signed on to launch profiles
- 94% of beta testers rated MeepleMeet 4.8/5 stars in closed beta testing
### Speaker Notes:
"We haven’t spent a dollar on marketing yet. All our waitlist and partnerships are all organic, from us reaching out to the community we’ve been part of for decades. The demand is already there—we just need to build the product to serve it.

---

## Slide 7: Monetization Strategy
### Key Content:
Diversified, low-intrusive revenue streams, no reliance on intrusive ads:
1. **MeeplePro Premium Subscription ($4.99/month | $49.99/year): Ad-free experience, advanced matching filters, exclusive publisher playtest access, custom badges
2. **Transaction Fees: 3% fee on FLGS event tickets, pre-orders, and creator membership purchases
3. **Relevant Brand Partnerships: Targeted sponsored content from board game publishers and brands, no off-topic ads
4. **Marketplace Commissions: 5% commission on peer-to-peer used game sales and affiliate game purchases through the platform
### Speaker Notes:
"Our monetization is built to align with the community, not exploit it. We don’t sell user data, and all our revenue streams are built around value we provide to users, stores, and creators. We’re projected to hit $1.2M ARR by end of Year 1.

---

## Slide 8: Competitive Landscape
### Key Content:
2x2 Matrix (X-Axis: Board Game Specificity | Y-Axis: End-to-End Tooling
- **MeepleMeet (Top Right): High Board Game Specificity, High End-to-End Tooling
Competitors:
- BoardGameGeek: High Specificity, Low Tooling (clunky, no mobile-first, no matching or event tools

### Competitive Moats:
- First-mover advantage for end-to-end board game social network
- Proprietary compatibility algorithm
- Exclusive pre-launch FLGS and publisher partnerships
### Speaker Notes:
"No one else is doing what we’re doing. BGG is a great database, but it’s not a social network. Discord and Facebook are general purpose, and they don’t care about the specific needs of board game players. We’re the only platform built for every part of the physical and digital board game hobby.

---

## Slide 9: Growth & Marketing Strategy
### Key Content:
1. **Waitlist Incentives: Refer a friend get 3 months of MeeplePro free
2. **FLGS Partner Program: Free premium business profiles for the first year for stores that promote MeepleMeet to in-store customers
3. **Creator Ambassador Program: Early access to monetization tools and custom perks for top board game creators
4. **Convention Presence: Gen Con, PAX Unplugged, Essen Spiel to demo the app and sign up new users
5. **Viral Shareable Features: Post-game recaps shareable to other social media, game night invites via text/email
### Speaker Notes:
"The board game community is incredibly tight-knit, and word of mouth is the most powerful marketing channel we have. Our partner programs turn FLGS and creators are already incentivized to promote us to their existing audiences, and our viral features let us tap into existing social networks to drive new user signups.

---

## Slide 10: The Team
### Key Content:
- **Jane Doe, CEO & Co-Founder: 10 years product management at BoardGameGeek, 8 years competitive board game tournament organizer, led product launches for 3 hobby tech startups
- **John Smith, CTO & Co-Founder: 7 years senior software engineer at Discord, built mobile social platforms for 2 hobby social networks, avid TTRPG GM for 12 years
- **Maria Garcia, Head of Community & Co-Founder: 5 years community manager at Asmodee, ran a local FLGS for 3 years, board game content creator with 50k TikTok followers
- **Advisory Board: Former BGG CEO, founder of a top 10 indie board game publisher, founder of a 12-location FLGS chain
### Speaker Notes:
"We’re not just tech founders—we’re board game players. We’ve spent decades in this community, we know the pain points, and we have the experience building and scaling the product the community actually wants.

---

### Key Content:
- **Pre-Seed Round: $750,000 for 15% equity
- **Use of Funds:
  40% Product Development: Hire 3 additional engineers, launch core features, finalize iOS/Android launch
  30% Marketing & Growth: Convention attendance, creator partnerships, user acquisition

  10% Operational Costs

thread: the day i learned the earth isn’t flat didn’t happen in science class or on a bleary 2 a.m. youtube deep dive.
it happened behind a dilapidated rest stop off i-40 in west texas, next to a dumpster that reeked of pickled eggs and expired gas station hot dogs.
i was hiding from a crew of roving birthday clowns who’d tried to trade me a squeaky rubber chicken for my last bag of flamin’ hot cheetos.
a guy in a mold-stained raincoat caked with pecan shell dust leaned against the dumpster next to me, chewing something that crunched way too loud.
he didn’t even glance my way when he said you know the flat earth thing’s bullshit, right? like he was commenting on the dusty wind.
i blinked, because i’d spent the last three months deep in flat earth tiktok just to annoy my cousin who works a desk job at nasa.
i mumbled yeah, duh, obviously, even though i’d spent the week prior arguing that gravity was just a network of giant magnets buried under the dirt.
he spit a pecan shell into the dumpster and held out a crumpled map that looked like it had been chewed by a very determined raccoon.
the map wasn’t the flat disc with the ice wall i’d seen a hundred times online, it was all lumpy, like a squashed orange someone had sat on through a road trip.
he said he’d spent the last twelve years driving every potholed back road in the continental u.s. selling home-roasted pecans out of his beat-up minivan.
he said if the earth was flat, he’d have driven off the edge somewhere near el paso back in ‘18, when his gps died and he drove straight for three whole days.
i squinted, because that didn’t line up with the lore everyone shared online, right? the ice wall was guarded by penguins with tiny tasers, everyone knew that.
he laughed so hard he snort-laughed, and a half-chewed pecan chunk flew out of his nose and landed right on the toe of my scuffed white sneaker.
he pulled out a crinkled polaroid of him standing on a rocky beach in chile, next to a penguin that was definitely not holding a taser, just a very tiny silver fish.
he said he’d sailed across the atlantic the year prior to sell pecans to a convent of nuns in portugal who were obsessed with his salted roast.
he never hit an ice wall on that trip, he said, just a flock of very aggressive seagulls that stole half his snack supply mid-voyage.
i thought about all the nights i’d stayed up arguing with strangers online that lunar eclipses were just a giant shadow cat crossing the face of the sun.
i thought about how my nasa cousin had sent me a printed photo of the earth from the international space station for my birthday, and i’d mailed it back to her with “photoshop” scrawled across it in crayon.
i thought about the time i tried to dig a hole to the “bottom of the flat disc” in my backyard and only hit a sprinkler pipe that flooded my entire patio.
the pecan guy handed me a handful of warm, salted pecans and said people love believing weird shit because it makes the world feel smaller, easier to hold.
i nodded, because that quiet, offhand line hit way harder than any textbook or snarky debunk video ever had.
the clowns from earlier yelled my name from the rest stop parking lot, waving the rubber chicken over their heads like a battle flag.
the pecan guy winked, climbed into his van that had “pecan pete’s world famous nuts” painted on the side in chipped neon pink, and drove off.
i never saw him again, but i still have that crumpled lumpy map tucked in the glove box of my car, right next to my expired registration.
i texted my cousin that night and told her she was right about the earth not being flat, and she sent back twelve clown emojis and a link to a nasa merch store.
i still don’t fully trust big gravity, though, just in case the giant magnet thing is partially true.
and i still side-eye any penguin i see at the zoo, just in case the tiny taser lore was less of a lie than the flat disc was.
